briefs.title: Misenchanted, Not Disenchanted: Is the Meaning Crisis a Story We Tell Ourselves?
briefs.body:
Every generation seems to discover that it lives at the end of meaning. Podcasts, books and op-eds describe a civilization that has lost its myths, its rituals and its sense of the sacred, and they usually end by recommending a return to something older. It is a compelling story, which is exactly why it deserves scrutiny.

James Croft, a humanist university chaplain, spent a long conversation on the Unsolicited Advice channel doing that. He does not deny that people are struggling. He sees it every day with students who are anxious about the future, about mental health, about whether they will have the lives they imagined. What he questions is the diagnosis, and above all the cure.

## The idea: the meaning crisis as an iatrogenic illness

Croft summarizes the standard narrative in three beats: symptoms (loneliness, mental illness, a sense that life is pointless), a diagnosis (the secular world is disenchanted, hollowed out, a famine of the spirit, to borrow the phrasing he quotes from John Vervaeke) and a cure (recover what we lost, often traditional religion, national identity or traditional gender roles). He accepts the first beat. Loneliness has worsened, particularly among young adults since Covid, and polls show a slight rise in people who say their lives are less meaningful than they'd like.

The second beat is where he parts ways. Secular life, he argues, is not a degraded version of something better we once had. It abounds with opportunities for beauty, significance and purpose. We have simply been encouraged to look at it wrongly. His coinage is that our world is not disenchanted but misenchanted: we are held by bad stories, bad habits of attention and bad institutions that put us out of tune with each other and with the world. And the meaning crisis discourse is, in his words, one of the major misenchantments. It is iatrogenic, a condition created by the treatment. Tell a young person that secular life is empty and they may begin interpreting their own life that way.

His second move is to trace the symptoms to ordinary, heterogeneous causes rather than one metaphysical rupture: economic insecurity and rising interest rates, housing costs, job precarity as AI advances, and parents who fear their children will be worse off. These are real pressures, he says, and they aren't solved by recovering a lost cosmos.

His third move is historical. The story of lost wholeness requires that people in the past were broadly existentially fulfilled, and Croft doubts the evidence. The past looks tidy because we know how it ended. Kierkegaard in Denmark and Dostoevsky in Russia wrote in crisis terms; Luther clearly wasn't spiritually content; the printing press triggered its own information-overload despair. We also never hear from the illiterate underclass who made up most of any society. A crisis that is unique to now, he suggests, needs proof that there was no crisis then.

He adds a philosophical argument from Martin Hägglund, whom he calls perhaps the greatest humanist philosopher writing today. If we lived in an eternal heaven where nothing could go wrong, our choices would mean nothing, because there would be no scarcity of time and no possibility of failure. Meaning depends on finitude and frailty. So what religious people want from heaven is really more of this life, and the hunger for an insuperable bedrock is a mistake.

## Our analysis

The strongest part of Croft's case is the iatrogenic point, which has real support in how framing affects people: labels shape self-interpretation, and a narrative that says your life is empty can be sticky. It also lines up with the long literature on declinism and the 'golden age' fallacy, and with the way every era from the printing press to the smartphone has produced a story of lost attention and lost depth. His historical sampling argument, that we only hear from the literate, is a good example of survivorship bias in the record.

Where it needs care: first, 'misenchantment' risks becoming unfalsifiable. If bad stories cause the pain and good stories cure it, any person who still suffers must be telling themselves the wrong story, which is a dismissive thing to say to someone dealing with loneliness or housing stress. Croft partly guards against this by insisting the material causes are real. Second, there's a measurement gap. Some evidence of declining religious participation alongside rising loneliness is not trivial, and a single poll uptick can't prove or refute either side. Third, his diagnosis shares a family resemblance with Viktor Frankl's insistence that meaning is found in commitments rather than given, and with Charles Taylor's account of the secular age, which treats secularism as a changed experience of meaning rather than its absence. Reading Croft alongside Taylor is more useful than treating them as opponents.

For work, the practical transfer is about narrative management. Teams and individuals also fall into crisis stories: the industry is dying, culture was better before, nothing means anything since the reorg. Ask what evidence supports the story of decline, whether previous generations felt the same, and which concrete, fixable pressures sit underneath the vague dread. Then act on the concrete ones.

The takeaway: take the symptoms seriously, distrust grand explanations that happen to flatter whoever is selling the cure, and put your energy into re-attuning to what's already in front of you: relationships, craft and commitments that matter precisely because they can fail.
briefs.highlight: Humanist chaplain James Croft argues that the 'meaning crisis' story popularised by thinkers like John Vervaeke is itself part of the problem. Its symptoms are real, he says: loneliness, anxiety, economic insecurity. But telling people secular life is hollow can make them read their lives that way. Croft calls the narrative iatrogenic, an illness caused by its own cure, and says our world is not disenchanted but misenchanted: out of tune with the beauty, purpose and hope already around us.

briefs.title: The Sublime You Stopped Noticing: Why Wonder Fades When Everything Is Easy
briefs.body:
You probably took a flight this year and spent it looking at a screen. Robert Greene's recent conversation with Ryan Holiday starts from that small, everyday waste and works outward to a claim about how we live: we are surrounded by experiences that earlier humans would have found overwhelming, and our access to them has dulled our capacity to be moved.

The conversation circles Greene's new book on the sublime, and it leans on historical imagination. It is a good exercise in its own right, so it's worth following his reasoning before testing it.

## The idea: wonder is a perishable capacity

Greene begins with the vanished cities of the past. The conquistadors who first entered Tenochtitlan, he says, wrote that they felt as though they were in a dream, a fairy tale: a city on water, with canals, gardens on rooftops and gleaming white temples, all built from one material. Not a trace remains. His point is that places like that, or ancient Babylon with its beveled houses angled to catch the light, or Athens under Pericles, were beautiful in ways we cannot recover, and we also do not know what their feeling was like from the inside, because it was all the people there knew. By contrast, he says, the modern city is a mess of mismatched glass buildings, noise and smell.

Holiday pushes back with Margaret Thatcher's reaction to Phoenix, where she saw unplanned sprawl as wonderful because it was spontaneous, humans doing what humans do, whereas Jane Jacobs would read the same scene differently. Greene agrees, and concedes a point central to his book: the sublime is everywhere, even in a decrepit building, because it is poignant and full of emotion. The issue is perception, not inventory.

The sharpest example is flight. Marcus Aurelius, Greene notes, advised taking the view from above, imagining yourself a bird looking down on the world, but even he could hardly climb higher than the Acropolis. Until the age of airplanes and, earlier, the first balloonists in 1780s France, almost no human being had looked down on the earth from altitude. Today nearly everyone has, and Greene thinks it is almost entirely lost on us. The airplane window is a shortcut to a view that took centuries of philosophy to approximate, and because we did not work for it, we do not feel its value. He cites Charles Lindbergh, who, flying over a luxury cruise ship on his Paris flight, thought of everyone who had suffered across the ocean in tiny boats and hoped flying would never become so comfortable that passengers forgot what they were on.

Greene ties this to childhood. As a boy he stared out of airplane windows and, at about five, remembers driving toward San Francisco and seeing the city's lights beyond the Golden Gate Bridge as a fairy tale. His thesis in the book is that because we once knew that kind of experience, we are unconsciously haunted by its absence, and that this missing wonder is a source of a lot of modern misery and depression.

## Our analysis

The idea holds up in a specific, modest form: effort and scarcity amplify attention. Psychologists call the underlying effect hedonic adaptation, the tendency of any stable pleasure to fade into background, and it's why new apartments and new phones stop delighting us. Greene's examples fit it well. Stoic practice already contains the remedy: Seneca and Epictetus advised premeditatio malorum and voluntary discomfort precisely to restore appreciation for what's taken for granted. The Marcus Aurelius 'view from above' exercise is a deliberate technique for manufacturing awe on demand.

It also connects to Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's work on attention and to recent research on awe, which finds that brief, deliberate encounters with vastness reduce rumination and increase a sense of connection.

Where it breaks: the claim that wonder's absence is a major cause of depression is far stronger than the evidence supports. Depression has biological, social and economic causes, and a nostalgic story about childhood can itself romanticise a past that wasn't wonderful for everyone, including the people who lived in those 'beautiful' ancient cities. Also, our guesses about how Babylon felt are imaginative reconstruction; it is as likely that residents were as numb to their surroundings as we are to ours, which would support Greene's mechanism rather than his nostalgia. The contrast between the beautiful past and the ugly present is partly survivorship: we remember the monuments, not the slums.

For work and life, the useful move is small and cheap. Treat wonder as a skill. Pick one thing per week that would astonish a person from 1900, such as a video call, a flight, or a pocket library, and spend two minutes attending to it without a screen. Schedule an occasional deliberate effort so ease does not erase meaning. And, at work, recall what it felt like in your first week: the vantage you had before familiarity set in is data about what your team or product actually looks like to a new person.

The takeaway: wonder is not gone; it is crowded out by convenience. Use the next flight, commute or sunrise as a drill, and look out of the window.
briefs.highlight: Robert Greene, on Ryan Holiday's Daily Stoic, argues that modern life is full of experiences that would once have felt sublime. Almost no one before 1930 saw the earth from the height of an airplane window, yet we scroll through the flight. Because the shortcut cost us no effort, he suggests, we miss its value. Greene thinks part of our modern restlessness is a haunting memory of childhood wonder we once had and lost, and that practising awareness of it can bring some of it back.
